# Do units move together? {#sec-dependence}

Units in a panel are rarely independent. States share a business cycle, and
neighbours share shocks. This chapter asks whether that co-movement is present
and how strong it is. The math lives in @sec-cd-theory.

## Question {#sec-dep-question}

Do the states' house prices move together more than chance allows?

## The test {#sec-cd-test}

Pesaran's CD averages the pairwise residual correlations
[@pesaran2015, p. 786]:

$$
CD = \sqrt{\frac{2T}{N(N-1)}} \sum_{i<j} \hat\rho_{ij}
  \;\xrightarrow{d}\; N(0,1).
$$

It sums raw $\hat\rho$, so correlations of opposite sign cancel. Unit roots
change the picture again; see @sec-ips.

### Run it {#sec-cd-run}

```r
data("HousePricesUS", package = "pder")
hp <- plm::pdata.frame(HousePricesUS)
plm::pcdtest(log(price) ~ 1, data = hp, test = "cd")
```

```
	Pesaran CD test for cross-sectional dependence in panels

data:  log(price) ~ 1
z = 162.63, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: cross-sectional dependence
```

### Read it {#sec-cd-read}

| Case | Data | CD | Reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rejects | Raw log prices | 162.63 | Strong co-movement |
| Does not reject | Simulated independent panel | 0.41 | Nothing to remove |
| Misleads | Two-way FE residuals | −1.20 | Cancelled, not absent |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Next
Rejects: measure the strength in @sec-exponent. Does not reject: standard
panel tools apply.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Book check
@pesaran2015 [p. 787] prints CD = 162.6 for this panel.
:::

## How strong is it? {#sec-exponent}

The exponent $\alpha$ says how many units a shock reaches. Near 1 means a
common factor; near 0.5 means local, spatial spillovers.

### Run it {#sec-exponent-run}

```r
dcce::csd_exponent(as_matrix(log(hp$price)))
```

```
alpha = 0.83 (se 0.04)
```

### Read it {#sec-exponent-read}

An $\alpha$ of 0.83 is strong dependence: remove common factors first.
